identity.title: Temperature & Humidity Display
identity.tagline: A little weather station for your desk: live temperature and humidity, always on screen.

goal: Read live temperature and humidity from a DHT11/DHT22 sensor and display both continuously on a 16x2 LCD — a compact standalone environment monitor, and the foundation the Smart Home Sensor Hub and WiFi Weather Station projects both build on later.
simpleSummary: Read live temperature and humidity from a DHT sensor and display both on a screen.
howItWorks: Unlike the analog or simple digital sensors used elsewhere in this encyclopedia, the DHT11/DHT22 communicates over a single wire using its own small timed-pulse protocol — it sends a whole packet of temperature and humidity data as a precise sequence of pulse lengths, which is why reading it requires a library rather than a plain digitalRead() or analogRead(). That library handles the pulse-timing and hands you back two plain numbers: temperature and humidity. From there, this project is mostly about display — formatting those two numbers clearly onto a small 2-line screen.
toolsNeeded: Arduino IDE (free, installed on your computer)
USB cable to connect the board to your computer
circuitDiagramCaption: DHT sensor's single data line on D2; LCD on the I2C bus (A4/A5).

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the DHT sensor's VCC to Arduino 5V, GND to GND, and DATA to D2.
wiringSteps.detail: Some DHT breakout boards include a pull-up resistor on the data line already; if you're using a bare 3-pin sensor with no breakout board, add a 10kΩ resistor between DATA and VCC.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the LCD's I2C backpack: GND to Arduino GND, VCC to 5V, SDA to A4, SCL to A5.
wiringSteps.detail: Identical wiring to the Ultrasonic Distance Meter project's LCD — if you've built that one already, this part is familiar.

wiringSteps.instruction: Install both the DHT sensor library and the LiquidCrystal_I2C library before uploading.
wiringSteps.detail: The DHT library ("DHT sensor library" by Adafruit, plus its "Adafruit Unified Sensor" dependency) is what turns the sensor's raw timed pulses into simple temperature/humidity numbers.

code.explanation: dht.readHumidity() and dht.readTemperature() do the heavy lifting, decoding the sensor's raw timed-pulse protocol into plain numbers. isnan() ("is not a number") checks for the read failing entirely — DHT sensors occasionally miss a read due to timing sensitivity, and printing a clear error is much friendlier than silently displaying stale or garbage values. The 2-second delay isn't arbitrary — it's the sensor's own minimum reliable sampling interval, not a display-refresh choice.

expectedBehavior: The LCD's top line shows current temperature, the bottom line shows humidity, both updating every two seconds. Breathing directly on the sensor should visibly raise the humidity reading within a few seconds.

troubleshooting.fix: Double-check the DATA wire is firmly seated and the correct DHT_TYPE constant (DHT11 vs DHT22) matches your actual sensor — using the wrong type is a common cause of consistent read failures.

troubleshooting.issue: Readings are implausible (e.g. -999 or wildly jumping around).
troubleshooting.fix: Add a 10kΩ pull-up resistor between DATA and VCC if your sensor is a bare 3-pin module without a breakout board — many boards include this already, bare sensors don't.
This is an LCD wiring/address issue, not a sensor issue — see the Ultrasonic Distance Meter project's troubleshooting for the same LCD setup.

extensions: Add a threshold alert (buzzer or LED) if humidity climbs above a level that risks mold growth.
Log readings with timestamps over Serial for a simple environment history.
Feed this same sensor into the Smart Home Sensor Hub project's WiFi dashboard.
Add a second DHT sensor in another room and display both readings side by side.
